questions.stem: Which condition increased ultraviolet radiation at the surface of early Earth?

options.text: The absence of free oxygen and therefore of a protective ozone layer
options.why: Atmospheric ozone forms from oxygen. With little free oxygen, early Earth had little ozone to absorb incoming ultraviolet radiation.

options.text: The accumulation of free oxygen released by the earliest photosynthetic organisms
options.why: Accumulating oxygen would allow an ozone layer to form and reduce ultraviolet penetration. It describes a later change caused by photosynthesis.

options.text: The removal of methane and carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere
options.why: Methane and carbon dioxide are linked to atmospheric warming in this topic. Removing them doesn’t explain the lack of ultraviolet protection.

options.text: The presence of an ozone layer composed mainly of carbon dioxide
options.why: Ozone consists of oxygen atoms, not carbon dioxide. An ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet radiation rather than increasing it.

questions.stem: Why are viruses classified as non-living in A2.1?

options.text: They lack cellular organization and depend on host-cell machinery for replication
options.why: Viruses can’t carry out independent metabolism or reproduce autonomously. They need a living host cell to make their components.

options.text: They contain no genetic information that can be inherited by descendants
options.why: Viruses contain DNA or RNA, so they do carry genetic information. Their dependence on host-cell machinery is the problem.

options.text: They are too small to perform any chemical reactions involving biological molecules
options.why: Size doesn’t determine whether something is living. Viruses can participate in chemical interactions but lack an independent cellular metabolism.

options.text: They reproduce by cell division only when environmental conditions become favorable
options.why: Viruses don’t reproduce by cell division. New viral particles are assembled from components made within an infected host cell.

questions.stem: Which result was obtained in the Miller–Urey experiment?

options.text: Amino acids and other carbon compounds formed from simpler substances
options.why: The experiment showed that biological building blocks could form abiotically when the chosen gas mixture received an energy input.

options.text: Self-replicating cells formed after the gases received electrical discharges
options.why: No cells or self-replicating systems formed. Electrical sparks helped produce much less complex carbon compounds.

options.text: DNA molecules formed and began directing the synthesis of proteins
options.why: The experiment didn’t produce DNA or a system for protein synthesis. It addressed the earlier formation of small carbon compounds.

options.text: Fatty-acid vesicles evolved by natural selection inside the apparatus
options.why: The reported result concerned abiotic production of carbon compounds. It didn’t demonstrate vesicle evolution or natural selection.

questions.stem: What is the strongest valid conclusion from the Miller–Urey experiment?

options.text: Abiotic production of carbon compounds is possible under some proposed prebiotic conditions
options.why: That conclusion stays within the evidence. The experiment tested one possible environment and produced carbon compounds without organisms.

options.text: The experimental gas mixture exactly reproduced the atmosphere of early Earth
options.why: The composition of the early atmosphere remains uncertain. An experimental model isn’t proof that every chosen condition existed.

options.text: The origin of self-replicating life from non-living matter has been demonstrated
options.why: The apparatus didn’t produce heredity, autonomous replication or cells. It tested one chemical step proposed before life.

options.text: Lightning was the only energy source capable of producing early organic molecules
options.why: Electrical sparks modeled one possible energy source. Ultraviolet radiation, heat and other energy sources could also drive prebiotic reactions.

questions.stem: Why can fatty acids form spherical bilayer vesicles in water?

options.text: Their hydrophilic regions face water while hydrophobic regions coalesce inward
options.why: Those interactions drive amphipathic molecules into bilayers. Closing into a sphere prevents hydrophobic regions at a bilayer edge from contacting water.

options.text: Their hydrophobic regions form hydrogen bonds with the surrounding water molecules
options.why: Hydrophobic regions interact poorly with water. They cluster away from it while the hydrophilic regions remain exposed.

options.text: Enzymes arrange each fatty acid into its genetically specified membrane position
options.why: This is self-assembly, so a pre-existing enzyme or genetic program isn’t required to position every molecule.

options.text: Electrical attraction places all hydrophilic regions inside an air-filled compartment
options.why: A vesicle has an aqueous interior, not an air-filled one. Hydrophilic regions face water on both sides of the bilayer.

questions.stem: What was the main biological importance of compartmentalization in protocells?

options.text: It allowed internal conditions and reactions to differ from the surroundings
options.why: A boundary can retain molecules, concentrate reactants and establish a distinct internal chemical environment.

options.text: It guaranteed that every membrane-bound structure could reproduce independently
options.why: A membrane doesn’t provide a replication system. Reproduction requires additional molecular processes for copying and inheritance.

options.text: It converted every molecule inside the compartment into genetic material
options.why: Enclosure doesn’t change all contents into information-carrying molecules. It keeps potentially useful molecules and reactions associated.

options.text: It prevented all substances and energy from crossing the outer boundary
options.why: A completely sealed compartment couldn’t obtain reactants or exchange energy. Membranes create selective boundaries, not total isolation.

questions.stem: Which combination of properties makes RNA a candidate for the first genetic material?

options.text: It can store sequence information and some RNA molecules can catalyze reactions
options.why: RNA can contribute to both heredity and catalysis. That combination could reduce the number of different molecular systems required in early life.

options.text: It is always double stranded and chemically more stable than DNA
options.why: Cellular RNA is usually single stranded and is generally less chemically stable than DNA. Greater stability helps DNA serve as modern long-term storage.

options.text: It contains amino acids that fold into active sites for metabolism
options.why: Proteins are polymers of amino acids. RNA is made from ribonucleotides, although its folding can still create a catalytic shape.

options.text: It can reproduce complete cells without templates, catalysts or energy
options.why: RNA replication requires chemical resources and a mechanism for templated copying. The hypothesis doesn’t give RNA unlimited autonomous reproduction.

questions.stem: Which observation in modern cells supports an ancient catalytic role for RNA?

options.text: Ribosomal RNA catalyzes peptide bond formation during translation
options.why: The ribosome retains RNA at the catalytic center of protein synthesis. This is evidence that RNA can act as a biological catalyst.

options.text: Messenger RNA permanently stores the complete genome of every cell
options.why: Modern cellular genomes are generally stored as DNA. Messenger RNA carries temporary copies of information for translation.

options.text: Transfer RNA catalyzes the replication of chromosomal DNA before division
options.why: Transfer RNA carries amino acids during translation. DNA polymerases and other proteins carry out chromosomal DNA replication.

options.text: Ribosomal proteins alone create every peptide bond during translation
options.why: Proteins support ribosome structure and function, but ribosomal RNA forms the catalytic center responsible for peptide bond formation.

questions.stem: Which statement defines LUCA most accurately?

options.text: The most recent ancestral population shared by all organisms alive today
options.why: LUCA is defined through the common ancestry of surviving organisms. It may have been a population rather than one individual cell.

options.text: The first self-replicating molecule that formed anywhere on early Earth
options.why: LUCA came after earlier prebiotic chemistry and probably after earlier living systems. It isn’t the first replicating molecule.

options.text: The only living lineage that ever evolved from non-living material
options.why: Other origins or early lineages may have occurred and then become extinct. Present evidence traces surviving life back to LUCA.

options.text: The earliest fossilized organism discovered in a hydrothermal vent deposit
options.why: No fossil has been identified directly as LUCA. LUCA is reconstructed from shared features and genomic comparisons.

questions.stem: Which evidence most directly supports common descent from LUCA?

options.text: A shared genetic code and conserved genes across cellular organisms
options.why: Extensive agreement in core information processing is expected if modern organisms inherited those features from common ancestry.

options.text: Different organisms occupying unrelated habitats throughout the modern world
options.why: Habitat diversity shows ecological adaptation, not common ancestry by itself. Molecular features shared across that diversity provide the evidence.

options.text: The formation of amino acids inside the Miller–Urey apparatus
options.why: Miller–Urey supports abiotic synthesis of building blocks. It doesn’t compare organisms or establish their common descent.

options.text: The spontaneous assembly of fatty acids into artificial laboratory vesicles
options.why: Vesicle assembly supports a possible step in protocell formation. It doesn’t show that present organisms share one ancestor.

questions.stem: What can the age of the oldest accepted biosignature establish?

options.text: Life existed by at least that date
options.why: A dated biosignature gives a minimum age for life. The biological system that produced it may have evolved much earlier.

options.text: Life originated at exactly that date
options.why: The earliest surviving evidence needn’t record the first life. Older evidence may have been destroyed, altered or never preserved.

options.text: LUCA divided into all modern species on that date
options.why: A biosignature doesn’t record every later divergence. LUCA and the diversification of modern lineages are inferred using additional evidence.

options.text: Every older carbon compound had a non-biological origin
options.why: An absence of accepted older evidence doesn’t prove an absence of older life. Preservation and interpretation are both limited.

questions.stem: How does a molecular clock estimate the time since two lineages diverged?

options.text: It relates sequence differences to an estimated rate of molecular change
options.why: Differences accumulate after divergence. A calibrated rate allows scientists to estimate how much time was needed to produce them.

options.text: It measures the radioactive decay of DNA preserved inside living cells
options.why: Molecular clocks compare inherited sequence changes. Radiometric dating instead measures radioactive isotopes in suitable geological materials.

options.text: It counts the number of cells produced by each lineage per year
options.why: Generation counts alone don’t reconstruct ancient divergence. The method depends on changes in homologous molecular sequences.

options.text: It assumes every organism has accumulated an identical number of mutations
options.why: Lineages and genes can change at different rates, which is a limitation. The method needs estimated rates and calibration, not identical totals.

questions.stem: Which finding would support the hypothesis that LUCA lived near hydrothermal vents?

options.text: Conserved genes indicate anaerobic, hydrogen-dependent metabolism suited to vent conditions
options.why: Genes inferred from shared sequences can reveal likely metabolic traits. Anaerobic use of hydrogen fits the chemistry around hydrothermal vents.

options.text: Recently evolved genes occur only in animals living near warm surface waters
options.why: Recent animal genes say little about LUCA. The relevant evidence must be ancient, conserved across major domains and tied to vent conditions.

options.text: Every modern organism requires oxygen for aerobic cellular respiration
options.why: Many organisms are anaerobic, and free oxygen was scarce on early Earth. Universal oxygen dependence isn’t a feature reconstructed for LUCA.

options.text: Miller–Urey products formed only when exposed to oxygen-rich seawater
options.why: The Miller–Urey atmosphere lacked free oxygen and didn’t test LUCA’s habitat. This option conflicts with both the setup and the evidence asked for.

questions.stem: A student claims that fossil-like structures in ancient vent deposits prove LUCA lived there. What is the best evaluation?

options.text: The structures support ancient life near vents but don’t identify it directly as LUCA
options.why: Location and age can support an early vent habitat. Identifying LUCA requires additional comparative genomic evidence and still remains an inference.

options.text: The structures prove the organisms were LUCA because all fossils preserve complete genomes
options.why: Ancient microscopic structures don’t preserve complete readable genomes. Their identity can’t be established that way.

options.text: The structures provide no evidence because minerals can never preserve biological material
options.why: Mineral precipitates can preserve biological shapes and chemical signatures. The limitation concerns interpretation, not an absolute lack of evidence.

options.text: The structures prove that hydrothermal vents created the first carbon compounds
options.why: Evidence of organisms near vents doesn’t establish where the earliest carbon compounds formed. Those are separate claims requiring different evidence.
